sets.title: Fish room moving upstairs
sets.passage:
Dear customers, from Monday 3 June our fish room will move from the back of the shop to a new room upstairs. The new room is bigger, so we can keep twice as many tanks. While we move the fish, the fish room will be closed for four days. You can still buy fish food, plants and nets at the front counter during this time. The fish room will open again upstairs on Friday 7 June. Thank you for your patience.

Ansel and Bree Ashwell

sets.title: Swallows over the front door
sets.passage:
To all library visitors: a pair of swallows has built a nest above our front door, and there are now four eggs in it. To keep the birds calm, the front door will stay closed until the end of July. Please use the side door next to the car park instead. It is open at the usual times. You can watch the nest from the window of the reading room, where we have left a book about swallows on the table.

Abri Bolin, librarian

sets.title: Ducklings in the courtyard
sets.passage:
On Tuesday morning, Bodie Aldwick arrived at school early and found the courtyard full of noise. A mother duck was walking in circles near the bench, and eleven small ducklings were following her. The courtyard had walls on all four sides, and the only way out was through the school building.

Mr. Beckford, the caretaker, came out with a cup of tea. "She nests here every spring," he said. "The pond is behind the gym, but the ducklings are too small to fly over the wall."

Bodie wanted to pick up the ducklings and carry them to the pond in a box. Mr. Beckford shook his head. "If we take them, she may leave them," he said. "We'll make a path for her instead."

Together they opened the doors of the long hallway that led to the gym. Mr. Beckford put chairs on both sides to make a narrow road. Then they stood far back and waited quietly.

For ten minutes the mother duck only watched. At last she stepped into the hallway, and the ducklings hurried after her in a tight line. She walked past the classrooms, through the gym and out the back door. Bodie counted the ducklings as they reached the grass by the pond. There were eleven.

At lunch, Bodie told the whole class what had happened. The next spring, Bodie was the first student to offer to help.

sets.title: Seahorse fathers
sets.passage:
Seahorses are small fish that live in warm, shallow seas in many parts of the world. They swim upright, and they use their curled tails to hold on to sea grass so that moving water does not carry them away. Because they are slow swimmers, they stay safe by hiding from danger rather than escaping it.

The most unusual thing about seahorses, however, is the way their young are born. In most animals, the mother carries the eggs or the babies. In seahorses, this job belongs to the father. The male has a pouch on the front of his body. During mating, the female places her eggs inside this pouch, and the male fertilizes them there.

For the next few weeks, the father carries the growing young. The pouch keeps them safe and helps control the water around them. When they are ready, he pushes them out into the sea. A single birth can produce dozens of babies, and in some kinds of seahorse it can be many hundreds.

After birth, the young seahorses are on their own. Their father gives them no more care, and most of them are eaten by other animals before they grow up. Only a very small number live long enough to become adults.

sets.title: Why woodpeckers do not get headaches
sets.passage:
Few birds put their heads through as much as woodpeckers do. To reach insects hidden under bark, to carve out holes for their nests and to send signals to other woodpeckers, they hammer their beaks against wood, sometimes more than ten times a second. Each strike ends in an abrupt stop, and the forces involved are far greater than those that would leave a person dizzy or injured. For a long time, the obvious question was how the birds manage to keep their brains safe.

The usual answer was that the woodpecker's head works like a shock absorber, a device that soaks up the energy of a blow so that less of it reaches whatever lies behind. Writers pointed to the spongy bone in the bird's skull and to a long, thin bone attached to the tongue, which curves around the back of the head and was thought to act like a safety belt. The idea was so widely accepted that engineers studied woodpeckers when designing helmets and protective cases for delicate equipment.

A few years ago, a team of biologists decided to test the idea directly. Instead of examining skulls in a laboratory, they filmed living woodpeckers of three different species with high-speed cameras while the birds pecked. By tracking points on the beak and near the eye, they could measure how quickly each part of the head slowed down at the moment of impact. If the skull were absorbing shock, the area around the brain should have slowed down more gently than the tip of the beak.

In the films, the beak and the braincase stopped almost together, which meant the head behaved less like a cushion and more like a stiff hammer. The researchers then used computer models to ask what a cushion would actually do. The answer was surprising: a head that absorbed shock would waste much of the energy of each strike, so the bird would have to hit far harder to break the same amount of wood. For an animal that can peck thousands of times a day, that would be a poor trade.

If the head is a hammer, why is the brain safe? The team's answer lies in size. A small brain is far less affected by a sudden stop than a large one, because the pressure that builds up inside a brain during an impact depends partly on its size. According to their calculations, the forces of ordinary pecking stay below the level likely to cause injury in a brain as small as a woodpecker's, although they would be dangerous for a brain the size of a human's. Their figures suggest that the birds would need to strike much harder before that safety margin began to disappear.

The study leaves room for the old features to matter, since the spongy bone may still help the skull resist damage over many years. But it changes the lesson engineers can take from the bird. A woodpecker shows how a small, stiff tool can strike safely, not how to cushion a large brain, and helmet designers may need to look elsewhere for ideas.

sets.title: The nest above the porch
sets.passage:
Every August my cousin Alvy and I spend two weeks at our grandmother's cottage near Ardmere, a village beside a wide, slow river. The cottage is small and old, and that summer it had a new resident. On the first morning, Alvy stepped out onto the porch with his toast and came straight back in, pale. Under the roof, just above the porch light, hung a grey ball the size of a melon, and wasps were drifting in and out of a hole near its bottom.

Alvy wanted it gone at once. He had been stung on the hand the summer before and had spent an afternoon with his arm in a bowl of ice. He found a long broom in the shed and announced that he would knock the nest into the river before breakfast was over. I was ready to help him. Our grandmother, who had been reading at the kitchen table, put down her book and asked us both to sit.

She told us that the wasps had been there since May and that she had been watching them all summer. They had built the nest themselves, she said, by chewing wood from the old fence into a kind of paper. Every morning she saw them carry green caterpillars back to it, and for the first time in years the cabbages in her garden had hardly a hole in them. "They feed those to their young," she explained. "I've had the best vegetables in the village."

Alvy pointed out that a wasp stings whoever is nearest, whatever garden it is protecting. My grandmother agreed. Knocking down a nest full of angry wasps, she said, was the surest way to be stung, and by more than one of them. Then she made an offer. The nest would last only until the cold weeks of autumn, when the colony would die out and the young queens would fly off to spend the winter somewhere else. Wasps build a fresh nest every year, so after that the old one could simply be taken down. If we could put up with them until then, she would make sure we stayed safe.

That afternoon we worked out the rules together. We moved the breakfast table from the porch to the shady side of the house, and we used the back door instead of the front one. My grandmother tied a red ribbon across the porch steps to mark the point where we had to stop. Alvy wrote the rules on a card in large letters and pinned it to the kitchen door, which I suspected was mostly so he could feel in charge.

By the second week, something had changed. Alvy, who had started the holiday armed with a broom, began sitting on the garden wall at a safe distance from the porch, watching the wasps come and go. He counted how many left the nest in a minute and wrote the numbers in a notebook. Nobody was stung that summer. On our last day he asked whether he could have the nest once it was empty, and my grandmother promised to post it to him in November, wrapped in newspaper. It arrived just before his birthday, as light as a dry leaf, and it now sits on a shelf above his bed.

to explain why he wanted the nest removed at once
to show why the writer refused to help him knock it down
items.correct_answer: to explain why he wanted the nest removed at once
items.why: Alvy wanted it gone at once. He had been stung on the hand the summer before
items.explanation: "to explain why he wanted the nest removed at once" is correct: the sentence comes straight after "Alvy wanted it gone at once" and gives the reason for it.

distractor_rationales.choice: to show that he was unafraid of the wasps on the porch
distractor_rationales.reason: "to show that he was unafraid of the wasps on the porch" is wrong: when he saw the nest he "came straight back in, pale".

distractor_rationales.choice: to show why the writer refused to help him knock it down
distractor_rationales.reason: "to show why the writer refused to help him knock it down" is wrong: the writer says "I was ready to help him".

distractor_rationales.choice: to explain why his arm was in a bowl of ice that morning
distractor_rationales.reason: "to explain why his arm was in a bowl of ice that morning" misreads the time: the "bowl of ice" was "the summer before", not that morning.

items.prompt: Which of the following best summarizes the story?
choices: A boy knocks a wasp nest into the river, and his grandmother explains why wasps are useful
A grandmother asks the boy to take down the nest so the cousins can use the porch
A grandmother persuades the cousins to keep the nest, and the writer starts studying the wasps
A family agrees to leave a wasp nest alone, and a boy's fear turns into interest
items.correct_answer: A family agrees to leave a wasp nest alone, and a boy's fear turns into interest
items.why: That afternoon we worked out the rules together.
items.explanation: "A family agrees to leave a wasp nest alone, and a boy's fear turns into interest" is correct: after "That afternoon we worked out the rules together", Alvy, who first "came straight back in, pale", ends up "watching the wasps come and go" and asks to keep the nest.

distractor_rationales.choice: A grandmother asks the boy to take down the nest so the cousins can use the porch
distractor_rationales.reason: "A grandmother asks the boy to take down the nest so the cousins can use the porch" misreads who wanted what: it was Alvy who "wanted it gone at once"; the grandmother offered to keep the nest "until the cold weeks of autumn", and the family moved the breakfast table "from the porch".

distractor_rationales.choice: A grandmother persuades the cousins to keep the nest, and the writer starts studying the wasps
distractor_rationales.reason: "A grandmother persuades the cousins to keep the nest, and the writer starts studying the wasps" is wrong in its second part: the one who studied the wasps was Alvy, who was "watching the wasps come and go" and "He counted how many left the nest in a minute".

distractor_rationales.choice: A boy knocks a wasp nest into the river, and his grandmother explains why wasps are useful
distractor_rationales.reason: "A boy knocks a wasp nest into the river, and his grandmother explains why wasps are useful" is wrong in its first part: he only "announced that he would knock the nest into the river"; the grandmother stopped him first.

items.prompt: According to the story, where did the wasps get the material for their nest?
choices: from the garden shed
from trees by the river
from the cabbage plants
from a wooden fence
items.correct_answer: from a wooden fence
items.why: by chewing wood from the old fence into a kind of paper
items.explanation: "from a wooden fence" is correct: they built the nest "by chewing wood from the old fence into a kind of paper".

distractor_rationales.choice: from the garden shed
distractor_rationales.reason: "from the garden shed" is wrong: the shed is where Alvy "found a long broom"; the nest wood came "from the old fence".

distractor_rationales.choice: from the cabbage plants
distractor_rationales.reason: "from the cabbage plants" is wrong: the cabbages are mentioned because they "had hardly a hole in them"; the nest was made "by chewing wood from the old fence".

distractor_rationales.choice: from trees by the river
distractor_rationales.reason: "from trees by the river" is wrong: the river is where Alvy wanted to "knock the nest"; the nest was made "by chewing wood from the old fence".

items.prompt: According to the grandmother, what will happen to the colony in autumn?
choices: It will come back to the same nest in spring
It will die, and its queens will go away for winter
It will move the nest to a warmer place
It will grow and build a second nest nearby
items.correct_answer: It will die, and its queens will go away for winter
items.why: the colony would die out and the young queens would fly off to spend the winter somewhere else
items.explanation: "It will die, and its queens will go away for winter" is correct: she says that in autumn "the colony would die out and the young queens would fly off to spend the winter somewhere else".

distractor_rationales.choice: It will move the nest to a warmer place
distractor_rationales.reason: "It will move the nest to a warmer place" is wrong: the old nest stays behind, since "Wasps build a fresh nest every year, so after that the old one could simply be taken down".

distractor_rationales.choice: It will come back to the same nest in spring
distractor_rationales.reason: "It will come back to the same nest in spring" is wrong: "Wasps build a fresh nest every year".

distractor_rationales.choice: It will grow and build a second nest nearby
distractor_rationales.reason: "It will grow and build a second nest nearby" is wrong: she says "the colony would die out", not grow.

items.prompt: In paragraph 6, the word "post" is closest in meaning to
choices: put up on a wall
send by mail
share online
assign to a job
items.correct_answer: send by mail
items.why: my grandmother promised to post it to him in November, wrapped in newspaper
items.explanation: "send by mail" is correct: she promised "to post it to him in November, wrapped in newspaper", and later "It arrived just before his birthday".

distractor_rationales.choice: put up on a wall
distractor_rationales.reason: "put up on a wall" is the meaning used for notices; the nest is sent "to him" and "arrived just before his birthday".

distractor_rationales.choice: share online
distractor_rationales.reason: "share online" is the meaning used for the internet; a nest "wrapped in newspaper" is a real object that "arrived".

distractor_rationales.choice: assign to a job
distractor_rationales.reason: "assign to a job" is the meaning used for jobs; it is the nest, "wrapped in newspaper", that is sent, not a worker.

items.prompt: In paragraph 5, the phrase "in charge" is closest in meaning to
choices: paying a fee
being accused
fully powered
in control
items.correct_answer: in control
items.why: which I suspected was mostly so he could feel in charge
items.explanation: "in control" is correct: Alvy "wrote the rules on a card" and pinned it up, "so he could feel in charge" of the rules.

distractor_rationales.choice: paying a fee
distractor_rationales.reason: "paying a fee" is the money meaning of "charge"; writing "the rules on a card" has nothing to do with paying.

distractor_rationales.choice: being accused
distractor_rationales.reason: "being accused" is the legal meaning of "charge"; Alvy "wrote the rules", and nobody accuses him of anything.

distractor_rationales.choice: fully powered
distractor_rationales.reason: "fully powered" is the meaning used for batteries; the phrase "feel in charge" is about a person, not a machine.
